analysis.one_liner: Bans corporate and union political committees, curbs franked mass mailings, and restricts gerrymandering.
analysis.headline: A sweeping campaign finance bill introduced by four Senate Republicans died in the Senate Rules Committee after two hearings, without ever getting a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overhauled how money reaches federal campaigns: it would shut down political committees run by corporations, labor unions, and trade associations, cap their contributions, tighten rules on bundled donations, and require unions to tell workers they can opt out of paying for political activity. It would also limit leftover campaign money, crack down on lawmakers' taxpayer-funded mass mailings, force disclosure of 'soft money' spending, and set standards against gerrymandered congressional districts. The bill was referred to the Senate Rules Committee, held two hearings, and never moved again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would get a political system less dependent on corporate, union, and trade-association committees, clearer disclosure of who paid for political ads, and more competitive House elections if district-drawing rules took hold. Taxpayers would save on lawmaker mass mailings, and employees who object to union political spending could reduce their dues. Political parties would gain, too, since the bill raises the amounts parties may spend on candidates.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the legal basis for political committees connected to corporations, labor unions, and trade associations, cutting off a major channel of special-interest money into campaigns.
It treats all money raised by a committee a candidate or officeholder controls as a contribution to that person, closing a loophole for raising beyond normal limits.

It bans unsolicited mass mailings at taxpayer expense, gives each lawmaker a mail budget based on population, and requires them to personally pay for postage above it, with quarterly cost reports published in the Congressional Record.

It sets standards for drawing congressional districts — equal population, compactness, minimal splits of counties and cities, and no dilution of voting strength — with fast federal court review that any voter can trigger.
It lets employees pay a reduced dues amount excluding political spending, and lets members deduct their share of union political spending from dues, with annual independent audits.
It lengthens the statute of limitations for campaign finance violations from three years back to five and lets the FEC share compliance files with the Attorney General for investigations.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, trade associations, and labor unions lose their political committees and a direct channel of campaign money. Incumbent lawmakers lose free taxpayer-funded mass mailings and the ability to bank surplus campaign funds. Political action committees of every stripe see their contribution limits cut in half.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises party coordinated-spending limits sharply — more than doubling the per-voter allowance and lifting the hard ceilings from $20,000 to $50,000 and $10,000 to $25,000 — shifting more political power to national and state party committees.

Banning union political committees silences organized labor's campaign voice at the same time it silences corporations', and independent expenditures outside party structures would remain a route for well-funded interests.
It offers no spending limits, no public financing, and no direct limits on individual donations, so critics could fairly say it trims around the edges rather than capping total campaign spending.

Redistricting rules like compactness and county-integrity standards can pull against creating districts where minority voters have a chance to elect their candidates, which is why the bill carries an explicit savings clause for the Voting Rights Act — an admission the two goals can collide.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: the bill would cut off a large, well-organized channel of special-interest money and an incumbent perk (franked mass mailings) that taxpayers fund, while leaving party spending and individual giving largely intact. Its union dues provisions protect individual workers but also weaken organized labor's political capacity, and its party-spending increases shift money toward national party machines. On balance it attacks special-interest and incumbent advantages more than it helps them, but it is not a complete reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Rules and Administration Committee — it got two hearings in early 1990, then nothing: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Dole introduced the bill on October 5, 1989, joined by Senators McConnell, Simpson, and McCain, describing its purpose as lessening the power of special economic interests and restoring competition to congressional elections.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
The Rules Committee held hearings on February 27 and March 1, 1990, but never reported the bill out.
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system's beneficiaries came out ahead: corporate, union, and trade-association political committees kept their fundraising channels, incumbent lawmakers kept taxpayer-funded franked mail, and candidates kept discretion over surplus campaign funds. Nobody had to defend the bill's restrictions on the floor.

for.name: Sen. Robert J. Dole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Comprehensive Campaign Finance Reform Act of 1989.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the majority
against.what_they_did: Held two hearings on the bill in February and March 1990, then never reported it to the floor or scheduled a markup.

against.name: Senate Majority Leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill's four Senate Republican sponsors were only 3 of 45 Republican cosponsors joining the sponsor, and the Democratic majority's Rules Committee let it die after hearings.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the legal basis for corporate- and trade-association-connected political committees and cuts multicandidate PAC contribution limits in half. Their spending power in federal elections is a direct rival to ordinary voters' influence, so their loss in this bill runs alongside the public's gain.

Unions lose their political committees and face new duties to notify workers they can't be forced to fund political activity, to offer agency fees, and to pass through pro rata dues reductions. Workers who object to union politics gain protections, while unions lose a political voice and money they had collected from members by default.

The bill raises coordinated-spending limits for party committees and lets candidates transfer unlimited surplus funds to party committees, channeling money toward party organizations. Parties are broad coalitions rather than narrow economic interests, but the change concentrates more campaign finance in national party hands.

The bill bans unsolicited franked mass mailings, gives each member a population-based mail budget, and makes members personally pay for postage beyond it — cutting off a publicly subsidized tool for self-promotion. Their interest in keeping the frank runs against taxpayers and challengers.
